lawyer:
Md Fazlul Karim, Advocate, instructed by Md Nowab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioner in both the petitions. 
Respondents in both the petitions ----- Not represented.
parties:
Fatema Bibi ------ Pre-emptor –Petitioner
vs.
Sree Manik Lal Somaddar & others ------ Pre-emptor-Respondent [in CP No. 578 of 1994]
full_judgment:
Lutfur Rahman, J. : Pre-emptor-petitioner filed Miscellaneous Case No. 3 of 1989 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the same was allowed by the trial Court. Against that judgment and order pre-emptee respondents preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 12 of 1991 and the same was allowed by the Subordinate Judge-In-Charge, Patuakhali, after setting aside the order of the trial Court. Against that judgment and order the pre-emptor petitioner filed two Civil Revision Cases being Civil Revision Nos. 1255 and 1256 of 1993 before the High Court Division and a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by a common judgment affirmed the decision of the Subordinate Judge and discharged the Rules. Pre-emptor petitioner is now seeking leave to appeal from the impugned judgment of the High Court Division by filing two separate leave petitions. 

 4. The trial Court, inter alia, found that the application for pre-emption was filed within time; that the kabala land is an agricultural land and that the pre-emptor though not a co-sharer is a contiguous land holder and allowed the pre-emption. The lower appellate Court held that the application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not maintainable as the land under pre-emption was non-agricultural land and that the pre-emptor was the owner of part of same plot No. 991 under khatian No.179 as she purchased land from Plot No. 991 with reference to SA Khatian No. 179, whereas the sale took place in respect of plot No. 991 under separate khatian No.185 which is recorded in the kabala of the pre-emptees. 

 5. Mr. Md Fazlul Karim, learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor petitioner submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted wrongly in holding that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the tenancy and thereby illegally dismissed the application for pre-emption. 

 6. It appears that pre-emption was sought for in respect of 0.05 acres of land in plot No.991 under SA Khatian No.185, whereas the pre-emptor purchased land from Plot No.991 appertaining to a separate SA Khatian No.179 and, as such, she was not a tenant in the case holding. The lower appellate Court found that the pre-emptor was not a tenant of the case holding No.185, whereas the respondent were co-sharers by purchase. Hence, the lower appellate Court rightly held that the pre-emptor had no locus standi to file the pre-emption case in respect of land of SA Khatin No.185. In both the khatians plot No. 991 is a common plot, but pre-emptor being not a co-sharer in SA Khatian No. 185 it was rightly held by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division that the application is not maintainable. The learned Single Judge also affirmed the finding of the lower appellate Court that the land in question being non-agricultural in nature, the application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not maintainable. The learned Single Judge having correctly decided the point of maintainability of the application for pre-emption the same calls for no interference.
